title: Rosaceae
wiki_lead:
Rosaceae (), the rose family, is a family of flowering plants that includes 4,828 known species in 91 genera.
The name is derived from the type genus Rosa. The family includes herbs, shrubs, and trees. Most species are deciduous, but some are evergreen. They have a worldwide range but are most diverse in the Northern Hemisphere.
Many economically important products come from the Rosaceae, including various edible fruits, such as apples, pears, quinces, apricots, plums, cherries, peaches, raspberries, blackberries, loquats, strawberries, rose hips, hawthorns, and almonds. The family also includes popular ornamental trees and shrubs, such as roses, meadowsweets, rowans, firethorns, and photinias.
Among the most species-rich genera in the family are Alchemilla (270), Sorbus (260), Crataegus (260), Cotoneaster (260), Rubus (250), and Prunus (340), which contains plums, cherries, peaches, apricots, and almonds. However, all of these numbers should be seen as estimates—much taxonomic work remains.

Among the most species-rich genera in the family are Alchemilla (270), Sorbus (260), Crataegus (260), Cotoneaster (260), Rubus (250), and Prunus (340), which contains plums, cherries, peaches, apricots, and almonds. However, all of these numbers should be seen as estimates—much taxonomic work remains.


Description
Rosaceae can be woody trees, shrubs, climbers or herbaceous plants. The herbs are mostly perennials, but some annuals also exist, such as Alchemilla arvensis.


Leaves
The leaves are generally arranged spirally, but have an opposite arrangement in some species. They can be simple or pinnately compound (either odd- or even-pinnate). Compound leaves appear in around 30 genera. The leaf margin is most often serrate. Paired stipules are generally present and are considered a primitive feature within the family, though they have been independently lost in many groups of Amygdaloideae (previously called Spiraeoideae). The stipules are sometimes adnate (attached surface to surface) to the petiole. Glands or extrafloral nectaries may be present on leaf margins or petioles. Spines may be present on the midrib of leaflets and the rachis of compound leaves.


Flowers
Flowers of plants in the rose family are generally described as "showy". They are radially symmetrical, and almost always hermaphroditic. Rosaceae generally have five sepals, five petals, and many spirally arranged stamens. The bases of the sepals, petals, and stamens are fused together to form a characteristic cup-like structure called a hypanthium. They can be arranged in spikes, or heads. Solitary flowers are rare. Rosaceae have a variety of color petals, but blue is almost completely absent.


Fruits and seeds
The fruits occur in many varieties and were once considered the main characters for the definition of subfamilies amongst Rosaceae, giving rise to a fundamentally artificial subdivision. They can be follicles, capsules, nuts, achenes, drupes (Prunus), and accessory fruits, like the pome of an apple, the hip of a rose, or the receptacle-derived aggregate accessory fruit of a strawberry. Many fruits of the family are edible, but their seeds often contain amygdalin, which can release cyanide during digestion if the seed is damaged.


Taxonomy


Taxonomic history
The family was traditionally divided into six subfamilies: Rosoideae, Spiraeoideae, Maloideae (Pomoideae), Amygdaloideae (Prunoideae), Neuradoideae, and Chrysobalanoideae, and most of these were treated as families by various authors. Later (1971), Chrysobalanoideae was placed in Malpighiales and Neuradoideae has been assigned to Malvales. Schulze-Menz, in Engler's Syllabus edited by Melchior (1964), recognized Rosoideae, Dryadoideae, Lyonothamnoideae, Spireoideae, Amygdaloideae, and Maloideae. They were primarily diagnosed by the structure of the fruits. More recent work has identified that not all of these groups were monophyletic. Hutchinson (1964) and Kalkman (2004) recognized only tribes (17 and 21, respectively). grok_lead: The Rosaceae family, commonly known as the rose family, is a diverse group of flowering plants in the order Rosales, encompassing approximately 100 genera and 3,000 species worldwide. These plants exhibit a wide range of growth habits, from herbaceous annuals and perennials to woody shrubs and small trees, and are characterized by their economic significance as sources of fruits, ornamentals, and medicinal compounds. Native primarily to the Northern Hemisphere temperate regions, with origins traced to areas like Central Asia for apples and Western China for pears, Rosaceae species play a vital role in global agriculture and horticulture. Morphologically, Rosaceae plants typically feature alternate leaves, often with stipules, that can be simple, compound, entire, or toothed. Their flowers are generally bisexual and radially symmetrical, with five separate sepals and five petals attached to a bowl-shaped hypanthium, numerous stamens, and superior ovaries that lead to diverse fruit types such as achenes, drupes, pomes, and aggregates. Fruits vary significantly across subfamilies: for instance, pomes in the Maloideae (like apples) and drupes in the Amygdaloideae (like peaches). Flower colors range from white and pink to yellow and red, often arranged solitarily or in clusters like racemes. Taxonomically, the family is divided into key subfamilies including Rosoideae (e.g., roses and strawberries), Amygdaloideae (e.g., cherries and almonds), and Dryadoideae, reflecting evolutionary adaptations such as whole-genome duplications that have contributed to their diversity. Phylogenetically, the ancestral form includes an apocarpous pistil with numerous free carpels, a trait retained in many Rosoideae species, while others have evolved syncarpous gynoecia. With the greatest species diversity in the Northern Hemisphere, Rosaceae has undergone adaptive radiation, leading to over 3,000 species that thrive in varied ecosystems from forests to grasslands. Economically, Rosaceae is one of the most important plant families, providing major crops such as apples ( Malus spp.), pears ( Pyrus spp.), peaches ( Prunus persica), strawberries ( Fragaria spp.), and roses ( Rosa spp.) for food, beverages, and perfumery (e.g., rose oil). These species are rich in antioxidants like ellagic acid, supporting health applications, and include timber sources as well as ornamental plants cultivated globally. The family's adaptability has made it a focus of genomic research, with sequenced genomes revealing transposable element bursts that influenced speciation events around 21 million years ago in lineages like apples.
